Idioms.phrase: 9-to-5 - An average job schedule.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He decided that he was going to look for a 9-to-5 job soon .

Idioms.phrase: A bad apple - A bad (or morally questionable) person within a group of good individuals, who might corrupt the entire group. Like a rotten apple in a barrel of good ones .
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Onlookers were worried that the entire group of trick-or-treaters was bad, but there were really only a couple of bad apples.

Idioms.phrase: A baker's dozen - Thirteen, or one more than an actual dozen (which is twelve).
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We went to the grocery store and bought a baker's dozen of chocolate chip muffins. We're looking forward to eating them later.

Idioms.phrase: A ballpark figure - An approximate figure.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, This is only a ballpark figure. It may not be very accurate once you add up all the numbers.

Idioms.phrase: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush - What you have at this moment carries more value than something you might obtain later.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jane asked me whether she should take the current job offer or wait for a better one. I told her to accept the current one. After all, a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.

Idioms.phrase: A bit/A little bit - To a small extent or a small amount.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I think I'll have just a little bit of cereal this morning. I'm not very hungry.

Idioms.phrase: A blessing in disguise - Something that seems bad initially, but that ends up having a positive outcome.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He was very upset about not getting the job, but it ended up being a blessing in disguise as he got a better one later on.

Idioms.phrase: A bone to pick - A reason why one is upset.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I have a bone to pick with you. I don't like the way you did this.

Idioms.phrase: A breath of fresh air - A person who is different from others in a very positive way. Everyone thought that Sasha was a breath of fresh air. She was so clever and friendly, and so different from anyone else they'd ever met.
A bunch of - A group of people, animals, or objects.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, A bunch of friends and I are going on a day trip tomorrow.

Idioms.phrase: A chip on your shoulder - You have a grievance of some kind—or an attitude—that you won't let go of.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Have you met Max? That guy has a real chip on his shoulder. He's always a bit arrogant and on the defensive.

Idioms.phrase: A day late and a dollar short - Too little and too late.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Elizabeth tried to hand in her assignment, but her teacher said it was a day late and a dollar short.

Idioms.phrase: A dime a dozen - A very common thing or occurrence.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Shirts in that style are a dime a dozen at the local mall.

Idioms.phrase: A doozy - Something incredible, usually in a negative way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, That storm the other day was a real doozy! I don't think I'll ever forget it. The thunder was terrible.

Idioms.phrase: A doubting Thomas - Someone who has a very skeptical attitude and who requires strong evidence to believe something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jonathan is very hard to convince about anything. He always wants evidence. He's a real doubting Thomas.

Idioms.phrase: A far cry from (something) - Has a great many differences from something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, That movie was a far cry from anything I would like. I just didn't enjoy it.

Idioms.phrase: A fifth wheel - Useless or unnecessary.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The team decided that the additional guest speaker was a fifth wheel and not necessary to include.

Idioms.phrase: A flash in the pan - Something that seems promising at first but ultimately doesn't deliver anything.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We were excited about what happened, but it ended up just being a flash in the pan. Nothing came of it.

Idioms.phrase: A fool and his money are easily parted - It's easy to convince a foolish person to give you their money for something silly.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I can't believe so many people have bought the product from that questionable infomercial. Well, you know what they say! A fool and his money are easily parted.

Idioms.phrase: A for effort - Made an excellent effort (but might not have done very well otherwise).
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I have to give the script writers an A for effort, but I don't feel that the program came together very well in the end.

Idioms.phrase: A fork in the road - A situation in which you can choose one path or another.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I think I've reached a fork in the road here. I don't know which direction to go.

Idioms.phrase: A good Samaritan - A person who helps others in need.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Shelly was always such a good Samaritan. She always helped people in need.

Idioms.phrase: A hang-up – Something—perhaps irrational—that consistently worries you.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Helen tended to be difficult to deal with. She had a lot of hang-ups, and it was easy to offend her.

Idioms.phrase: A hard nut to crack - Someone who is difficult to get to know or understand, or someone who is tricky to deal with.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Yes, I'm enjoying my new job. My boss, though, is a hard nut to crack. I'm having difficulty in understanding what he wants.

Idioms.phrase: A hot potato - An issue, probably from current events, that is causing a lot of discussion and controversy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The family tried to avoid bringing up political hot potatoes during the holidays.

Idioms.phrase: A kickback - A bribe or other illegal payment of money, usually offered to get someone to do something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The politician was known to be corrupt. It had been proven that he had accepted kickbacks from several people.

Idioms.phrase: A little bird told me – A person (possibly someone recognized by both participants in the conversation) who imparted the information in question.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, How did I find out that your sister is getting married? A little bird told me.

Idioms.phrase: A little learning is a dangerous thing - People who have only a limited understanding of something can be dangerous.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Some people are always promoting opinions that make me realize that a little learning can be a dangerous thing.

Idioms.phrase: A memory like a sieve - An inadequate memory.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I can't believe I forgot that! I have a memory like a sieve.

Idioms.phrase: A penny for your thoughts - Tell me your thoughts.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, You're very quiet today. A penny for your thoughts.

Idioms.phrase: A penny saved is a penny earned – If you save money right now, you will have more later.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Try to save more of your money. Remember that a penny saved is a penny earned.

Idioms.phrase: A perfect storm - When several things go wrong at once, creating the worst situation possible.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The family seemed to be experiencing a perfect storm of unfortunate events.

Idioms.phrase: A picture is worth a thousand words - It is more effective to show than it is to tell.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Look at the sad faces on everyone. They wouldn’t believe it if they hadn’t seen it. A picture is worth a thousand words.

Idioms.phrase: A piece of cake - Very easy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't worry about the exam. I took one for the same course last year and it was a piece of cake.

Idioms.phrase: A ray of sunshine - Someone who is always cheerful and makes other people feel more positive.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Audrey is a ray of sunshine. She is always so cheerful that she inevitably cheers me up as well.

Idioms.phrase: A rip-off - Something that costs too much for what it is really worth.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The coat was a rip-off. It was extremely expensive and ended up being low-quality.

Idioms.phrase: A screw loose - To be crazy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We thought he had a screw loose when we saw him dancing around as if his shoes were on fire!

Idioms.phrase: A screwup - A mistake.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It turned out that what they said in the announcement was a screwup! They're not really opening on August 15th.

Idioms.phrase: A sledgehammer to crack a nut - Using a disproportionate (and probably ineffective) solution for a problem.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I can't understand why Charles is doing such drastic things to try to solve a simple problem. It's like using a sledgehammer to crack a nut!

Idioms.phrase: A smart cookie - A clever and quick-thinking person.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, You're a really smart cookie, so you're sure to do well on the test if you study hard.

Idioms.phrase: A snowball effect – A series of events gain momentum and build upon one another, leading to a more impactful outcome.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Things started to go wrong; eventually, it seemed like they were dealing with a snowball effect.

Idioms.phrase: A snowball's chance in hell - No chance of something happening.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jake wants to travel this summer but there's not a snowball's chance in hell that he will get to.

Idioms.phrase: A stitch in time saves nine - Deal with the problem now because it will get worse if you leave it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Abby decided to deal with the problem and not leave it for later. After all, a stitch in time saves nine.

Idioms.phrase: A stone's throw - Very close by.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We had an awesome time on vacation! The hotel was just a stone's throw away from lots of the museums we were eager to visit.

Idioms.phrase: A storm in a teacup - A lot of fuss about an insignificant problem.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Jill and Amy got really upset about the issue but calmed down later on. They realized it was just a storm in a teacup.

Idioms.phrase: A storm is brewing - There is likely to be significant trouble in the near future.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Do you really think everything is okay? I have a feeling that if it is, it won't be for long. I think a storm is brewing.

Idioms.phrase: A surefire way - An approach that will definitely lead to something happening.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Failing to study early on in a course is a surefire way of getting a bad mark.

Idioms.phrase: A sweet tooth - To love sweet foods and flavors.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm afraid I have a terrible sweet tooth. I eat far too much cake and candy.

Idioms.phrase: A toss-up - Something that is difficult to decide.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She couldn't decide which of her friends had improved the most in their running skills. It was a toss-up!

Idioms.phrase: Absentminded - Gives the impression of not being aware of what is happening in the present moment.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He seemed a bit absentminded that day. His focus seemed to be somewhere else.

Idioms.phrase: Ace in the hole - A hidden, but very effective, method for winning a conflict.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My resume ended up being my ace in the hole when competing for the job. I was the most highly qualified.

Idioms.phrase: Ace up the sleeve - A hidden advantage in a competition.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, No, I'm not worried about the upcoming competition. I have an ace up my sleeve.

Idioms.phrase: Achilles' heel - A significant weakness and/or reason for potential downfall.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, His love of junk food was his Achilles' heel. It really was his downfall, as it greatly affected his health.

Idioms.phrase: Acid test - An important or critical test of something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Beth felt that their outing on the upcoming weekend would be the acid test for her friendship with Meredith. It would tell her whether the friendship could really continue.

Idioms.phrase: Across the board - In every area and/or in every way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We decided to change the rules for the contest across the board. They just weren't fair.

Idioms.phrase: Actions speak louder than words - A person's actions will give you a better idea of their character than their words.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My friend apologized for upsetting me, but I'm not sure if I believe that she will change yet. Actions speak louder than words.

Idioms.phrase: Add fuel to the fire - To make something even worse.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Maxine tried to help with the problem, but it turned out that her advice only added fuel to the fire.

Idioms.phrase: Add insult to injury - To worsen an already bad situation or cause more problems for someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I bought a new sweater that I thought was on sale, but they didn't give me the discount. To add insult to injury, they wouldn't give me a refund when I brought it back.

Idioms.phrase: Against the clock - Running out of time.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Madison was really rushing with the end of her exam. She was working against the clock.

Idioms.phrase: Ahead of schedule - To finish something earlier than the schedule requires.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Things are getting done ahead of schedule. Our boss is very pleased about that.

Idioms.phrase: All bark and no bite - Seems more intimidating than he, she, or it actually is.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't worry about Larry getting angry. He's a bit like his big dog. His bark is worse than his bite!

Idioms.phrase: All bets are off - Any existing agreements are discarded.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, When Angela found out that her friend had talked behind her back, she decided that all bets were off and she would do the same to her.

Idioms.phrase: All Greek to me - I don't understand it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm having a hard time understanding this instructions pamphlet. It's all Greek to me.

Idioms.phrase: All heart - To be very kind and loving to others. (This can sometimes be said in a sarcastic manner, in reference to a person who seems to be the opposite.)
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Abigail is a wonderful, caring person. She's all heart.

Idioms.phrase: All in the same boat - All in the same situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We are all in the same situation right now. Without a doubt, we are all in the same boat.

Idioms.phrase: All kidding aside - I was joking before, but now I'm going to speak seriously.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, So, do you think it would be okay if I spent all day, every day, at the beach this summer? But all kidding aside, I do want to spend a lot of time by the ocean this year.

Idioms.phrase: All over the map - Something (for example, a conversation) that doesn't stay on target with the primary topic or purpose—it’s a bit scattered in different directions.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We discussed the issue, but the conversation was all over the map. It wasn't very focused.

Idioms.phrase: All set - Ready to go or proceed.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Are you all set to go? We need to leave soon.

Idioms.phrase: All thumbs - Clumsy, especially with intricate tasks that require a lot of dexterity.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I ended up ruining my knitting project. I'm all thumbs with complicated things like that.

Idioms.phrase: All wet - Wrong to the extent of being unbelievable or just silly.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Harry really gets on my nerves sometimes. Some of the things he says are all wet. He tends to be silly.

Idioms.phrase: Along for the ride - To be present when something is happening, without actually participating in it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I thought that my friend wanted to come on the trip to keep me company and make me feel better, but it turned out that she was just along for the ride.

Idioms.phrase: An about-face - A sudden change, usually in the opposite direction.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She did an about-face on this topic a little while ago. She completely changed her position and opinions.

Idioms.phrase: An albatross around my neck - An encumbrance or significant burden.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Her illness was extremely persistent and difficult to deal with. It was like an albatross around her neck.

Idioms.phrase: An apple a day keeps the doctor away - Eating healthfully, for example eating apples, will help to preserve good health.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My co-workers always joke about how I bring an apple for lunch every day. But I tell them that an apple a day keeps the doctor away.

Idioms.phrase: An old head on young shoulders - Someone who seems to have more perception and wisdom than most other people the same age.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Marissa was an old head on young shoulders. She was only seventeen years old but seemed so wise and sensible.

Idioms.phrase: An old soul - Someone who seems to have more emotional insight and wisdom than other people the same age.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Everyone said that Henry was an old soul. He seemed to have so much wisdom and insight for a sixteen-year-old boy.

Idioms.phrase: An open book - Someone who is extremely open about themselves.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It was very easy to get to know Hannah. She was an open book and made friends easily.

Idioms.phrase: An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure - It's better to deal with a problem early. It will be more difficult to fix if you leave it for later.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Henry decided to go to the doctor about his headaches. It probably wasn't anything serious, but an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

Idioms.phrase: Are you kidding me? - Are you joking? Often said to express disbelief, even if the speaker doesn't think that the other person is joking.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Are you kidding me? I can't believe that what you just said is true. Is it?

Idioms.phrase: Armchair quarterback - A person who offers opinions and advice but shows no evidence that they actually have any necessary knowledge and/or skill. Especially used with regard to American football.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Bob wouldn't keep quiet during the football game; he constantly talked about what the players were doing wrong. He's such an armchair quarterback.

Idioms.phrase: Armed to the teeth - To be heavily armed.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I watched that war movie I mentioned last night. All the characters were armed to the teeth.

Idioms.phrase: Around-the-clock - At every time of day and night.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Their boss seems quite unreasonable. It appears he expects an immediate response from them around-the-clock!

Idioms.phrase: As busy as a bee - Very busy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm as busy as a bee this morning. I've run lots of errands and completed lots of tasks.

Idioms.phrase: As easy as ABC - Very simple and easy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't worry about learning how to ride a bike. It's as easy as ABC once you get going.

Idioms.phrase: As easy as pie - Extremely easy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, No problem. I'll show you to how to do this tomorrow. Don't worry! It's as easy as pie.

Idioms.phrase: As genuine as a three-dollar bill - Fake, as three-dollar bills do not exist.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Xavier was showing us many of his antiques, telling us that they are rare and expensive. In my opinion, though, some of them are about as genuine as a three-dollar bill.

Idioms.phrase: As happy as a clam - Happy and content.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't worry about the kids. They're as happy as clams playing video games in the other room!

Idioms.phrase: As quiet as a mouse - Very quiet and reserved.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She is as quiet as a mouse. It seems like she hardly ever speaks.

Idioms.phrase: As rare as hen's teeth - Extremely rare or non-existent.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, No, I have never seen that animal even though it's supposed to live around here. I've found they're as rare as hen's teeth.

Idioms.phrase: As right as rain - It's good or perfect.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Maggie asked me how my work was going and I told her the truth, that it's as right as rain.

Idioms.phrase: As the crow flies – Either in a straight line or directly, without the use of roads.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The mall is only two miles away, as the crow flies. It's takes longer to get there when you take certain routes.

Idioms.phrase: As white as a sheet/as white as a ghost - Extremely pale, so much so that it causes concern.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, What's wrong? You look as white as a sheet! Are you ill? Has something terrible happened?

Idioms.phrase: At best - In the best-case scenario.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, At best, I can say that he was kind of creative in his essay. It wasn't very good, overall.

Idioms.phrase: At-large - At liberty when one shouldn't be. For example, if a criminal has escaped from the authorities and his whereabouts are unknown.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The news bulletin said that the individual who escaped from prison is still at-large.

Idioms.phrase: At least - At a minimum.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It's disappointing that she can't go with you this time, but at least she might be able to next time.

Idioms.phrase: At loggerheads - In conflict with each other.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The two co-workers were at loggerheads on the project. They just couldn't agree on the correct direction.

Idioms.phrase: At my wits' end - Getting extremely frustrated and close to becoming angry.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Janette explained that she was at her wits' end with a few of her friends. They were very difficult to deal with and she felt she couldn't communicate with them.

Idioms.phrase: At the bottom of the totem pole - Having a low-status position, especially at work.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Michael decided against giving any suggestions about how things should be done at work. After all, he was still at the bottom of the totem pole and didn't have much influence.

Idioms.phrase: At the crack of dawn - Extremely early in the morning.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They need to wake up at what seems like the crack of dawn in order to get there in time.

Idioms.phrase: At the drop of a hat - Right away and without hesitation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Juliana was really impatient as she waited for her friends to join her, but they couldn't just come over at the drop of a hat.

Idioms.phrase: At the end of your rope - Reached the limit of endurance and/or patience with something or someone.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The teacher felt like she was almost at the end of her rope with some of the students. They were very difficult to deal with in class and liked to test her patience.
